questions.q: What is the key difference between a time-series regression and a cross-sectional regression in asset pricing?
options: Time-series regression requires more computing power
A time-series regression fixes one asset and uses many periods to estimate its beta; a cross-sectional regression fixes one period and uses many assets to estimate the price of risk
Cross-sectional regression can only be run on bonds
There is no meaningful difference; the two terms describe the same procedure
questions.explain: Time-series regression answers 'what is this asset's beta'; cross-sectional regression answers 'is beta compensated, and by how much' at a given point in time.

questions.q: What problem arises from running a single naive cross-sectional regression of average returns on previously estimated betas?
options: The regression cannot be computed at all
Errors-in-variables: the betas are themselves noisy estimates, which biases the slope and makes the regression's own standard errors unreliable
It requires factor data that doesn't exist
It only works for a single asset at a time
questions.explain: Because estimated betas carry their own estimation error, using them as regressors in a single cross-sectional regression understates the true uncertainty in the risk-premium estimate.

questions.q: In the Fama-MacBeth procedure, how is the final standard error of the risk-premium estimate computed?
options: From the residuals of the single, final time-series regression
As the standard deviation of the period-by-period cross-sectional lambda_t estimates, divided by sqrt(T)
It is assumed to be zero since lambda is an average
From a bootstrap over individual stock-level residuals only
questions.explain: The Fama-MacBeth standard error comes from how much the period-specific risk-premium estimates vary across time: std(lambda_1...lambda_T) / sqrt(T).

questions.q: In the worked example, the Fama-MacBeth risk premium (0.00674) matched the naive single cross-sectional regression's point estimate exactly, but the standard errors differed sharply (0.00268 vs 0.00064). Why?
options: The naive regression used a different sample of data
The naive regression implicitly treats each asset as an independent observation, understating uncertainty, while Fama-MacBeth's standard error reflects actual period-to-period variability
The Fama-MacBeth standard error formula has a typo and should match the naive one
Because the factor returns were not normally distributed
questions.explain: The point estimates coincide mathematically, but Fama-MacBeth's standard error honestly reflects how much the risk premium estimate bounces around across periods, while the naive approach's small standard error ignores cross-asset correlation within each period.

questions.q: Why does the Fama-MacBeth risk-premium estimate in the worked example (0.00674) land close to the factor's own realized mean return (0.00635)?
options: This is a coincidence specific to this random seed
Because the lesson used only one asset
In a one-factor design, each period's cross-sectional slope is, in expectation, that period's factor return itself, so averaging those slopes recovers the factor's realized mean
Because the betas were all set equal to 1.0
questions.explain: With a single common factor, the period-by-period cross-sectional regression slope is mathematically tied to that period's factor return, so the Fama-MacBeth average tracks the factor's realized mean return.
